subject: SLA availability ceiling & monthly credit cap request
messages:
From: Emily Kaplan <emily.kaplan@cloudsoft.com>
To: aisha_rahman@redwood.ai
Cc: Cloudsoft Procurement <procurement@cloudsoft.com>
Date: Tue, 25 Aug 2026 09:18:00 -0700
Subject: SLA: availability ceiling & monthly credit cap request

Hi Aisha,

Thanks again for the call this morning —Cloudsoft's technical and procurement teams reviewed the standard Redwood SLA and we have two asks we'd like to table for the final contract: 1) an availability floor change for our production tier from 99.95% to 99.9% to reflect our multi-region failover design, and 2) a fixed monthly credit cap rather than uncapped pro-rata credits (we're proposing a cap equal to 25% of the monthly service fee).

The rationale on both: our internal risk modeling assumes transient region failovers will cause short availability dips that our app can tolerate (we'll failover to a standby region), and an uncapped credit exposure complicates our CFO approval. We prefer a predictable worst-case credit. We're happy to accept slightly looser latency SLOs during scheduled maintenance windows if that helps.

Attached is a redline of your template that shows the two changes (proposed SLA redline and a sample monthly-credit table). Can you let me know if Redwood would consider a credit cap at that level or an alternative fixed bucket approach? We'd like to move to legal by next week if possible.

Thanks,
Emily Kaplan
Cloudsoft Inc — Head of Platform Partnerships

Attachments: cloudsoft-proposed-SLA-redline.pdf (PDF, 42 KB), monthly-credit-schedule.xlsx (XLSX, 12 KB)
From: aisha_rahman@redwood.ai
To: Emily Kaplan <emily.kaplan@cloudsoft.com>
Cc: Cloudsoft Procurement <procurement@cloudsoft.com>, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 25 Aug 2026 11:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA: availability ceiling & monthly credit cap request

Hi Emily —

Appreciate the clear note and the redlines. Short answer: we can discuss both items, though they raise slightly different product and commercial tradeoffs. I'll sync internally today and propose a small counter that preserves predictable exposure for you while protecting our ability to remediate large incidents.

High-level thinking:
- Availability floor: moving to 99.9% for your prod tier is feasible if Cloudsoft will accept a reduced uptime-based credit rate in the 99.9–99.95 band and keep the same failure reporting procedures. This aligns to customers who run active/passive multi-region.
- Monthly credit cap: we don't typically accept fixed caps on credits for platform-wide outage classes, but we can offer a structured cap tied to incident classification (e.g., maintenance vs. platform-wide outage) with a hard cap for maintenance-related impacts.

I'll pull Ben in to propose specific banding, and loop in Legal (Laura) to start drafting language. Can we schedule a 30-minute alignment tomorrow at 10am PT?

Best,
Aisha Rahman
Director, Customer Success — Redwood Inference

From: ben_carter@redwood.ai
To: aisha_rahman@redwood.ai, laura_bennett@redwood.ai, monica_patel@redwood.ai
Date: Tue, 25 Aug 2026 13:07:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: SLA: availability ceiling & monthly credit cap request

Aisha / Laura / Monica —

Quick notes after skimming the redline: I like the idea of an incident-classification linked cap. Proposed counter we can take to Cloudsoft tomorrow:
1) Keep standard uptime bands (99.99 / 99.95 / 99.9) but alter payout multipliers for active/passive multi-region customers: reduce payout in the 99.9 band by 50% vs. standard.
2) Offer a monthly maintenance credit cap equal to 25% of monthly fees for scheduled or maintenance-class incidents. For platform-wide outages (severity P0/P1), credits remain uncapped but prorated per-incident with a de-escalation curve after repeated incidents.
3) Add explicit language about latency SLOs during maintenance windows and a 72-hour incident reporting SLA to qualify for credits.

This preserves a hard cap for maintenance (their ask) while leaving protection for them on true platform failures. From a commercial perspective, it also limits predictable exposure.

If that sounds ok I can draft the short paragraph and the modified credit table. Laura — can you flag any legal redlines you'd expect here? Monica — can you confirm whether CS will require runbook updates or a service advisory cadence for the active/passive behavior?

-Ben
VP, Sales Operations
From: laura_bennett@redwood.ai
To: ben_carter@redwood.ai, aisha_rahman@redwood.ai, monica_patel@redwood.ai
Date: Wed, 26 Aug 2026 09:14:00 -07:00
Subject: RE: SLA: availability ceiling & monthly credit cap request

Ben —

High-level legal take: the structure Ben proposes is workable. Points to add/confirm in the contract draft:
- Clear definitions for incident classes (maintenance / regional failover / platform outage) with examples.
- An explicit exceptions list (force majeure, customer's misconfiguration, third-party cloud provider maintenance) — we should keep these to standard carveouts.
- A modest reporting and remediation cooperation clause (48–72 hours) and an audit process for credit disputes.
- Cap language must be asymmetric: maintenance cap can be accepted, but platform outage cap needs an escape clause (e.g., Redwood may propose a different remedy in lieu of credits if absolute caps apply to platform outages, which we'd prefer to avoid).

I can have a tracked-wording snippet by EOD and a short appendix that maps the credit table to incident classes.

—Laura
Associate GC, Redwood Inference

Aisha / Ben / Laura —

Thanks — that approach seems reasonable and gets to the predictability our CFO wants while preserving protection for true platform incidents. Two quick asks from Cloudsoft: 1) can we get the proposed amended credit table (with the maintenance cap row) in your next redline, and 2) can we confirm the 10am PT alignment tomorrow? Procurement would like the cap language in plain English and an example calculation.

If you send the updated table and the short legal snippet, we should be able to sign off and feed to our legal tomorrow afternoon.

Appreciate the quick turnaround,
Emily
